title: The north falls (2 Kings 17)
hook: Assyria takes Samaria and the northern tribes are carried away and scattered

segments.voice: Yesterday, four outcasts at a city gate found an empty camp and said: this day is a day of good tidings, and we hold our peace. Did you pass some good news along? Today, the news is the opposite. Day seven hundred seventy-seven.

Look back over this week. Elisha asks for pi shnayim, and his teacher's cloak falls to him. A woman in Shunem builds a little room on her roof for a holy man. A proud general is told to wash in the Jordan, because a captive girl spoke up. A frightened servant has his eyes opened to help he couldn't see. Four lepers carry good news to a starving city. All of it happens in the northern kingdom, Israel, with its capital at Samaria. And today, in one chapter, that kingdom ends.
screen: `A WEEK IN THE NORTH.` → `CLOAK, ROOF, RIVER, GATE.` → `TODAY IT ENDS.`

segments.voice: The last king of the north is named Hoshea. He stops paying tribute to Assyria and looks to Egypt for help. The king of Assyria marches in, besieges Samaria, and takes it. Then he carries the people of Israel away into Assyria, and settles them in distant places the text names: Halah, and Habor by the river of Gozan, and the cities of the Medes. And then the chapter does something unusual. It stops telling the story and starts explaining it. Why did this happen? The writer's answer is long and blunt: the people had turned to other gods, though prophets had warned them again and again. The text says the Lord had warned Israel and Judah by every prophet and every seer, saying turn from your evil ways. They would not hear. And then one sad line: "there was none left but the tribe of Judah only." The north is gone. Next the king of Assyria brings in people from other lands to live in the empty towns of Samaria. The map is redrawn. Those carried away never come back in the story. The book of Kings simply goes on with Judah. Later readers would call them the lost tribes, and tradition tells stories about where they went. The prophets didn't let the north be forgotten, though. Ezekiel is told to take two sticks, one for Judah and one for Joseph, and join them into one in his hand. Jewish tradition keeps that hope alive: one day, the scattered come home. The lost tribes are lost to the record. They were not lost to memory.
screen: `HOSHEA TURNS TO EGYPT.` · `SAMARIA TAKEN, ISRAEL CARRIED AWAY.` · then, large: `NONE LEFT BUT THE TRIBE OF JUDAH.` · then: `THE STORY GOES SILENT.` · `TWO STICKS JOINED IN ONE HAND.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: think of those lost to history. Let your shoulders drop. Bring to mind people whose names nobody wrote down: great-great-grandparents you can't name, a town that isn't on the map anymore, the workers who built a place you walk past every day. You don't need faces or details. Just let them be real for a moment. People who cooked, worried, laughed, and were carried off by time. With each slow breath, hold one of them in mind. If you pray, you can remember them before God. The bell holds the time.
Hoshea, the last king of the northern kingdom, whose revolt against Assyria brought the siege that carried Israel away and ended the north.
Your line: the lost tribes. Today, ask an older relative or friend one name from the family you've never heard, and write it down. Day seven hundred seventy-seven.

howItsDone: Jews read 2 Kings 17 as part of the Former Prophets, and the hope that the scattered tribes will one day be gathered appears in the prophets and in Jewish prayer.

fork.setup: you're the writer of Kings. the northern kingdom has just fallen. what do you write next?
options: stop the story and explain why it happened.
follow the exiles to their new lands.
fork.reveal: the chapter pauses the story for a long explanation: the people turned away, though every prophet and seer had warned them.

original.note: Hebrew: exile, the word Jewish tradition uses for life scattered away from the land.

trapdoor: what you thought: the lost tribes are a mystery story.
what it means: the north is carried away, and the book of Kings goes on with Judah alone.
what a scholar hears: 2 Kings 17 pauses its own story to explain the fall, and the prophets keep a hope of reunion.

sources.quoted: there was none left but the tribe of Judah only.

notes: The index hook gives a date (around 722 BCE); per the claims rule the script leaves the date out because 2 Kings 17 does not state it.
Quotation of 2 Kings 17:18 is from KJV; JPS 1917 wording is believed identical. Keeper may prefer citing JPS 1917.
'Some communities in faraway places tell that they descend from them' is deliberately vague; Keeper may want to name examples or cut.
Week-end look back covers days 771–776 (Elisha cycle and the four lepers).
'Jewish tradition keeps that hope alive' (ingathering of exiles): Keeper may wish to name the weekday Amidah blessing.

Editor: fixed the place list to match 17:6 (Habor is by the river of Gozan, not a separate place) in teach and myth; cut the unsourced claim about where the phrase 'lost tribes' comes from and about faraway communities' descent, replaced with 'tradition tells'.

Audit: quotation now cited to JPS 1917 (path standard); review paraphrase of 7:9 corrected to 'this day is a day of good tidings'; hook fixed so Elisha asks for the double portion before the cloak falls (2:9–13); varied the templated 'Settle, and breathe' practice opener used on all ten days 777–786.
